nodes.statement: A basic non-abelian example is provided by the Heisenberg group. This group has appeared already in many works in higher-order Fourier analysis since ; recall that it is the group of 3times 3 upper unitriangular real matrices H= 1 & R & R\\[0.1em]0 & 1 & R\\[0.1em] 0 & 0 & 1 vspace0.05cm. A special case of what we prove in this paper is that, as a nilspace, the Heisenberg group is isomorphic to a nilspace expressible in terms of structures which are among the most basic ones in nilspace theory, and which play a key role in this paper, namely the nilspaces D_k(R). (Given any abelian group Z and kinN, we denote by D_k(Z) the k-step nilspace associated with the filtered group (Z,Z_bullet), where the filtration Z_bullet=(Z_i)_igeq 0 consists of Z_i=Z for ileq k and Z_i=\id\ otherwise; see .) Indeed, the group nilspace consisting of H equipped with the Host-Kra cubes (relative to the lower-central series) is isomorphic to the product nilspace F=D_1(R^2)times D_2(R) (in this special case, this can be checked directly, an isomorphism being varphi:(x,y,z)in F mapsto 1 & x & z\\[0.1em]0 & 1 & y\\[0.1em] 0 & 0 & 1 in Hvspace0.05cm). The Heisenberg nilmanifold is the quotient space H/Gamma where Gamma is the discrete Heisenberg group 1 & Z & Z\\[0.1em]0 & 1 & Z\\[0.1em] 0 & 0 & 1 vspace0.05cm. Using this isomorphism, it is easily seen that H/Gamma is isomorphic (as a nilspace) to the quotient of F by the action of the group generated by the following transformations on F, which are specific examples of nilspace translations (see ): alpha(x,y,z)=(x+1,y,z) and beta(x,y,z)=(x,y+1,z+x). Indeed, these two translations correspond (via the isomorphism varphi) to the right multiplications in H by the elements 1 & 1 & 0\\[0.1em]0 & 1 & 0\\[0.1em] 0 & 0 & 1 and 1 & 0 & 0\\[0.1em] 0 & 1 & 1\\[0.1em] 0 & 0 & 1 respectively, and these elements generate Gamma.

(Given any abelian group $\mathrm{Z}$ and $k\in\mathbb{N}$, we denote by $\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z})$ the $k$-step nilspace associated with the filtered group $(\mathrm{Z},\mathrm{Z}_\bullet)$, where the filtration $\mathrm{Z}_\bullet=(\mathrm{Z}_i)_{i\geq 0}$ consists of $\mathrm{Z}_i=\mathrm{Z}$ for $i\leq k$ and $\mathrm{Z}_i=\{\mathrm{id}\}$ otherwise; see \cite[\S 2.2.4]{Cand:Notes1}.) Indeed, the group nilspace consisting of $\mathcal{H}$ equipped with the Host-Kra cubes (relative to the lower-central series) is isomorphic to the product nilspace  $F=\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{R}^2)\times \mathcal{D}_2(\mathbb{R})$ (in this special case, this can be checked directly, an isomorphism being $\varphi:(x,y,z)\in F \mapsto \begin{psmallmatrix} 1 & x & z\\[0.1em]0  & 1 & y\\[0.1em] 0 & 0 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix}\in \mathcal{H}\vspace{0.05cm}$). The Heisenberg nilmanifold is the quotient space $\mathcal{H}/\Gamma$ where $\Gamma$ is the \emph{discrete} Heisenberg group $\begin{psmallmatrix} 1 & \mathbb{Z} & \mathbb{Z}\\[0.1em]0  & 1 & \mathbb{Z}\\[0.1em] 0 & 0 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix}\vspace{0.05cm}$. Using this isomorphism, it is easily seen that $\mathcal{H}/\Gamma$ is isomorphic (as a nilspace) to the quotient of $F$ by the action of the group generated by the following transformations on $F$, which are specific examples of \emph{nilspace translations} (see \cite[\S 3.2.4]{Cand:Notes1}): $\alpha(x,y,z)=(x+1,y,z)$ and $\beta(x,y,z)=(x,y+1,z+x)$. nodes.statement: A free nilspace is a direct product (in the nilspace category) of finitely many components of the form D_i(R) and D_i(Z) where iin N. We say that a free nilspace is discrete if it is a direct product of components of the form D_i(Z), and that it is continuous if it is a direct product of components of the form D_i(R).
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:free-nil-intro}
A \emph{free nilspace} is a direct product (in the nilspace category) of finitely many components of the form $\mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{R})$ and $\mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z})$ where $i\in \mathbb{N}$. We say that a free nilspace is \emph{discrete} if it is a direct product of components of the form $\mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z})$, and that it is \emph{continuous} if it is a direct product of components of the form $\mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{R})$.
nodes.clean_text: A free nilspace is a direct product (in the nilspace category) of finitely many components of the form D_i(R) and D_i(Z) where iin N. We say that a free nilspace is discrete if it is a direct product of components of the form D_i(Z), and that it is continuous if it is a direct product of components of the form D_i(R).
nodes.label: def:free-nil-intro

nodes.statement: Let F=D_1(R)times D_2(Z)times D_3(Rtimes Z). Then the translation group Theta(F) consists of functions of the form \[ (x,y,z,t)mapsto left(x+a_1,\; y+a_2,\; z+a_3+a_4x+a_5binomx2+a_6y,\; t+a_7+a_8yright) \] where a_1,a_3,a_4,a_5,a_6in R and a_2,a_7,a_8in Z. Informally speaking, the variable xin D_1(R) is continuous and thus it will only appear in higher-order continuous components. Moreover, it is of step 1, so in the D_3(R) component (say) it can appear as a polynomial of degree only at most 2, in order to satisfy the general rule given in Theorem , according to which the ``step" of the variable (here the step of x is 1) times the degree of its involving polynomial should be less than the step of the coordinate in which this polynomial appears (namely here the step of D_3(R), which is 3). Similarly, y is of step 2 and thus (by the same rule) it can only appear in D_3(R) or D_3(Z) as a polynomial of degree at most 1; similarly for t.

Let $F=\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{R})\times \mathcal{D}_2(\mathbb{Z})\times \mathcal{D}_3(\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{Z})$. Then the translation group $\Theta(F)$ consists of functions of the form
\[
(x,y,z,t)\mapsto \left(x+a_1,\; y+a_2,\; z+a_3+a_4x+a_5\binom{x}{2}+a_6y,\;  t+a_7+a_8y\right)
\]
where $a_1,a_3,a_4,a_5,a_6\in \mathbb{R}$ and $a_2,a_7,a_8\in \mathbb{Z}$. Informally speaking, the variable $x\in \mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{R})$ is \emph{continuous} and thus it will only appear in higher-order \emph{continuous} components. Moreover, it is \emph{of step 1}, so in the $\mathcal{D}_3(\mathbb{R})$ component (say) it can appear as a polynomial of degree only at most 2, in order to satisfy the general rule given in Theorem \ref{thm:decrip-trans-group}, according to which the ``step" of the variable (here the step of $x$ is 1) times the degree of its involving polynomial should be less than the step of the coordinate in which this polynomial appears (namely here the step of $\mathcal{D}_3(\mathbb{R})$, which is 3). Similarly, $y$ is of \emph{step 2} and thus (by the same rule) it can only appear in $\mathcal{D}_3(\mathbb{R})$ or $\mathcal{D}_3(\mathbb{Z})$ as a polynomial of degree at most $1$; similarly for $t$.

nodes.name: Fiberwise discrete and cocompact actions on free nilspaces
nodes.statement: Let F be a free nilspace and let Gamma be a fiber-transitive group on F. We say that Gamma is fiber-discrete if for every jin[k], the group eta_j(Gamma)cap Theta_j(F_j) is a discrete subgroup of Theta_j(F_j)cong Z^a_jtimes R^b_j. We say that Gamma is fiber-cocompact if for every jin[k], the group eta_j(Gamma)cap Theta_j(F_j) is cocompact in Theta_j(F_j).
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:FDCA}
Let $F$ be a free nilspace and let $\Gamma$ be a fiber-transitive group on $F$. We say that $\Gamma$ is \emph{fiber-discrete} if for every $j\in[k]$, the group $\eta_j(\Gamma)\cap \Theta_j(F_j)$ is a discrete subgroup of $\Theta_j(F_j)\cong \mathbb{Z}^{a_j}\times \mathbb{R}^{b_j}$. We say that $\Gamma$ is \emph{fiber-cocompact} if for every $j\in[k]$, the group $\eta_j(\Gamma)\cap \Theta_j(F_j)$ is cocompact in $\Theta_j(F_j)$.

We say that Gamma is fiber-cocompact if for every jin[k], the group eta_j(Gamma)cap Theta_j(F_j) is cocompact in Theta_j(F_j).
nodes.label: def:FDCA

nodes.statement: Note that given a fiber-transitive group Gamma, if it is fiber-discrete then it is a discrete subgroup of Theta(F) in the usual sense; see Lemma . However, note that Gamma being fiber-cocompact does not imply that Gamma is a cocompact subgroup of Theta(F); see Example . On the other hand Gamma being fiber-cocompact does imply that the topological space F/Gamma is compact; this is clear in Example , and in general it follows from Lemma and Corollary .

\label{def:CRDCnilpair}
Let $(G,G_\bullet)$ be a degree-$k$ filtered Lie group such that for each $i\in[k]$ the subgroup $G_i$ is closed in $G$. Let $(K,\Gamma)$ be a groupable nilpair in $(G,G_\bullet)$. For each $i\in [k]$ let $K_i=K\cap G_i$, $\Gamma_i=\Gamma\cap G_i$. We say the nilpair $(K,\Gamma)$ is \emph{closed right-discrete} if for every $i\in[k]$ the group $(KG_{i+1})/G_{i+1}$ is a closed subgroup of $G/G_{i+1}$ and $K_i \Gamma_i G_{i+1} /(K_iG_{i+1})$ is a discrete subgroup of $G_i/(K_iG_{i+1})$. nodes.statement: On the abelian group (Z,+) let us define the topology tau generated by all the sets \n\ for nin Zsetminus\0\ and the sets \0,3^m,3^m+1,ldots\ for min N. It can be checked that this topology is textsclch. Hence, in particular this is a metric space. We claim that (Z,tau) satisfies that for all nge 0, the set C^n(D_1(Z)) is closed in Z^dbn, but (Z,tau,+) is not a topological group. In order to prove that the cube sets are closed, note that it suffices to prove that C^2(D_1(Z)) is closed (since every higher-dimensional cube set is an intersection of preimages of 2-dimensional cube sets by continuous coordinate-projection maps). Let ((x_n,y_n,z_n,t_n))_n be a sequence in C^2(D_1(Z)) (that is, satisfying x_n+y_n=z_n+t_n for each n) and converging to some limit (x,y,z,t). We want to prove that x+y=z+t. Note that in this topology there are two types of convergent sequences. If bin Zsetminus\0\, then b_nrightarrow b means that b_n=b for n sufficiently large. If b=0, then b_nrightarrow b means that either b_n=0 for n large enough, or there exists a subsequence (b_n_m)_m such that b_n_m=3^iota(m) for some strictly increasing function iota:Nrightarrow N. Thus, if (b_n) converges then either b_n is eventually constant or we can restrict to a subsequence such that b_n_m=3^iota(m) for an increasing iota. Coming back to the convergent sequence (x_n,y_n,z_n,t_n), we have the following exhaustive cases. In the first case, all four component sequences are eventually constant, and we then have the desired closure. In a second case, only one of the sequences has a strictly increasing subsequence, and then (relabeling the subsequence), we have x_n=3^iota(n), and y_n,z_n,t_n are eventually constant. We would then have 3^iota(n) equal to the constant z+t-y, which is impossible for n large enough. In the third case, two of the component sequences in the tuple (x_n,y_n,z_n,t_n) have a strictly increasing subsequence. Then note that the only subcase here that is not obviously impossible is when these two components are on different sides of the equation x_n+y_n = z_n+t_n. Suppose that these components are x_n and z_n. Passing to a subsequence if necessary, we may assume that x_n=3^iota_1(n). If, on this subsequence, the component z_n becomes eventually constant (zero), then we are back into the previous case, yielding a contradiction. Otherwise we can pass to a further subsequence in which x_n=3^iota_1(n) and z_n=3^iota_2(n). Then, as y_n and t_n are eventually constant, for n large enough they are equal to y and t respectively. But now, if we write the equation 3^iota_1(n)+y=3^iota_2(n)+t in base 3, it follows that as iota_1 and iota_2 are strictly increasing, the equation can hold for all such large enough n only if y=t and iota_1(n)=iota_2(n). Thus, the limit of (x_n,y_n,z_n,t_n) is (0,y,0,y), which is in C^2(D_1(Z)). The case when three of the component sequences have infinite increasing subsequences (and the fourth one is eventually constant) is treated similarly, considering subcases, in each of which either one obtains a contradiction or a conclusion confirming the desired closure. The case when all four sequences have a strictly increasing subsequence leads to the limit (0,0,0,0), which is in C^2(D_1(Z)) as required. Finally, note that (Z,tau,+) is not a topological group, because the sequence (3^n,3^n) converges to (0,0) but 3^n+3^n=2cdot3^n diverges as nrightarrowinfty.

On the abelian group $(\mathbb{Z},+)$ let us define the topology $\tau$ generated by all the sets $\{n\}$ for $n\in \mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}$ and the sets $\{0,3^m,3^{m+1},\ldots\}$ for $m\in \mathbb{N}$. It can be checked that this topology is \textsc{lch}. Hence, in particular this is a metric space. We claim that $(\mathbb{Z},\tau)$ satisfies that for all $n\ge 0$, the set $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{Z}))$ is closed in $\mathbb{Z}^{\db{n}}$, but $(\mathbb{Z},\tau,+)$ is not a topological group. 

In order to prove that the cube sets are closed, note that it suffices to prove that $\mathrm{C}^2(\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{Z}))$ is closed (since every higher-dimensional cube set is an intersection of preimages of 2-dimensional cube sets by continuous coordinate-projection maps). Let $((x_n,y_n,z_n,t_n))_n$ be a sequence in $\mathrm{C}^2(\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{Z}))$ (that is, satisfying $x_n+y_n=z_n+t_n$ for each $n$) and converging to some limit $(x,y,z,t)$. We want to prove that $x+y=z+t$. Note that in this topology there are two types of convergent sequences. If $b\in \mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}$, then $b_n\rightarrow  b$ means that $b_n=b$ for $n$ sufficiently large. If $b=0$, then $b_n\rightarrow b$ means that either $b_n=0$ for $n$ large enough, or there exists a subsequence $(b_{n_m})_m$ such that $b_{n_m}=3^{\iota(m)}$ for some strictly increasing function $\iota:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow \mathbb{N}$. Thus, if $(b_n)$ converges then either $b_n$ is eventually constant or we can restrict to a subsequence such that $b_{n_m}=3^{\iota(m)}$ for an increasing $\iota$. Coming back to the convergent sequence $(x_n,y_n,z_n,t_n)$, we have the following exhaustive cases. In the first case,  all four component sequences are eventually constant, and we then have the desired closure. In a second case, only one of the sequences has a strictly increasing subsequence, and then (relabeling the subsequence), we have $x_n=3^{\iota(n)}$, and $y_n,z_n,t_n$ are eventually constant. We would then have $3^{\iota(n)}$ equal to the constant $z+t-y$, which is impossible for $n$ large enough. In the third case, two of the component sequences in the tuple $(x_n,y_n,z_n,t_n)$ have a strictly increasing subsequence. Then note that the only subcase here that is not obviously impossible is when these two components are on different sides of the equation $x_n+y_n = z_n+t_n$. Suppose that these components are $x_n$ and $z_n$. Passing to a subsequence if necessary, we may assume that $x_n=3^{\iota_1(n)}$. If, on this subsequence, the component $z_n$ becomes eventually constant (zero), then we are back into the previous case, yielding a contradiction. Otherwise we can pass to a further subsequence in which $x_n=3^{\iota_1(n)}$ and $z_n=3^{\iota_2(n)}$. Then, as $y_n$ and $t_n$ are eventually constant, for $n$ large enough they are equal to $y$ and $t$ respectively. But now, if we write the equation $3^{\iota_1(n)}+y=3^{\iota_2(n)}+t$ in base 3, it follows that as $\iota_1$ and $\iota_2$ are strictly increasing, the equation can hold for all such large enough $n$ only if $y=t$ and $\iota_1(n)=\iota_2(n)$. Thus, the limit of $(x_n,y_n,z_n,t_n)$ is $(0,y,0,y)$,  which is in $\mathrm{C}^2(\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{Z}))$. The case when three of the component sequences have infinite increasing subsequences (and the fourth one is eventually constant) is treated similarly, considering subcases, in each of which either one obtains a contradiction or a conclusion confirming the desired closure. The case when all four sequences have a strictly increasing subsequence leads to the limit $(0,0,0,0)$, which is in $\mathrm{C}^2(\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{Z}))$ as required.

Finally, note that $(\mathbb{Z},\tau,+)$ is not a topological group, because the sequence $(3^n,3^n)$ converges to $(0,0)$ but $3^n+3^n=2\cdot3^n$ diverges as $n\rightarrow\infty$.

nodes.statement: Fix any xin X and let (y_n) be any sequence of points y_nsim_i x converging to some yin X. We just need to show that ysim_i x. This follows by definition of sim_i and the cube-set closure assumptions; indeed there is an (i+1)-cube c_n equal to x everywhere except at one vertex where it equals y_n, and the convergence of y_n to y implies that c_n converges to a map g that equals x everywhere except at one vertex where it equals y. By the closure of C^i+1(X) we deduce that g is a cube, which implies that ysim_i x as required. To see that the graph of sim_i is a closed subset of Xtimes X, the argument is similar: suppose that (x_n,y_n) is a convergent sequence in this graph, that is we have x_nsim_i y_n for all n and there is (x,y)in XtimesX such that (x_n,y_n)rightarrow (x,y) in Xtimes X. Now x_nsim_i y_n means there is an (i+1)-cube c_n equal to x_n at all vertices except at 1^i+1 where it equals y_n. The convergence (x_n,y_n)rightarrow (x,y) implies that (c_n) converges in X^dbi+1 to a map g equal to x at every vertex except at 1^i+1 where it equals y. By closure of C^i+1(X) we have that gin C^i+1(X), so (x,y) is in the graph of sim_i as required.

Fix any $x\in \mathrm{X}$ and let $(y_n)$ be any sequence of points $y_n\sim_i x$ converging to some $y\in \mathrm{X}$. We just need to show that $y\sim_i x$. This follows by definition of $\sim_i$ and the cube-set closure assumptions; indeed there is an $(i+1)$-cube $\mathrm{c}_n$ equal to $x$ everywhere except at one vertex where it equals $y_n$, and the convergence of $y_n$ to $y$ implies that $\mathrm{c}_n$ converges to a map $g$ that equals $x$ everywhere except at one vertex where it equals $y$. By the closure of $\mathrm{C}^{i+1}(\mathrm{X})$ we deduce that $g$ is a cube, which implies that $y\sim_i x$ as required.

To see that the graph of $\sim_i$ is a closed subset of $\mathrm{X}\times \mathrm{X}$, the argument is similar: suppose that $(x_n,y_n)$ is a convergent sequence in this graph, that is we have $x_n\sim_i y_n$ for all $n$ and there is $(x,y)\in \mathrm{X}\times\mathrm{X}$ such that $(x_n,y_n)\rightarrow (x,y)$ in $\mathrm{X}\times \mathrm{X}$. Now $x_n\sim_i y_n$ means there is an $(i+1)$-cube $\mathrm{c}_n$ equal to $x_n$ at all vertices except at $1^{i+1}$ where it equals $y_n$. By closure of $\mathrm{C}^{i+1}(\mathrm{X})$ we have that $g\in \mathrm{C}^{i+1}(\mathrm{X})$, so $(x,y)$ is in the graph of $\sim_i$ as required.

\label{def:fib-prod}
Let $\mathrm{X}, \mathrm{X}'$ and $\mathrm{Y}$ be nilspaces and let $\varphi:\mathrm{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{Y}$ and $\varphi':\mathrm{X}'\rightarrow\mathrm{Y}$ be fibrations. We define the \emph{fiber product} of $\mathrm{X}$ and $\mathrm{X}'$ as the nilspace consisting of the set $\mathrm{X}\times_{\mathrm{Y}}\mathrm{X}':=\{(x,x')\in \mathrm{X}\times\mathrm{X}': \varphi(x)=\varphi'(x')\}$ endowed with the cubes $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X} \times_{\mathrm{Y}} \mathrm{X}'):=\{(\mathrm{c},\mathrm{c}')\in \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})\times \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}'):\varphi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}=\varphi'\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}'\}$.

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:Cartan}
Let $B$ be a $G$-principal bundle. Let the action of $G$ over $B$ be given by $(g,b)\in G\times B\mapsto  gb\in B$. We say that the bundle is a \emph{Cartan principal bundle} if given the map $T:B\times G\rightarrow B\times B$ defined by $(b,g)\mapsto(b,gb)$ there exists a continuous map\footnote{Here the image ${\rm im}(T)$ is understood to have the subspace topology.} $R:{\rm im}(T)\rightarrow B\times G$ such that $R\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} T=\mathrm{id}_{B\times G}$.

That is, we shall use that there exists a covering of $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ by open sets $\{U_i\}_{i\in I}$ such for each $i$ there is a map $\pi_{k-1}^{-1}(U_i)\rightarrow  U_i \times\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$ that is a homeomorphism which is also $\mathrm{Z}_k$-equivariant.

Fix any $x\in\mathrm{X}$. We now show that for small enough neighborhoods of $x$, their images under $\varphi$ are open. Let $V\subset \mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ be any open neighborhood of $\pi_{k-1}(\varphi(x))$ such that there is a $\mathrm{Z}_k$-equivariant homeomorphism $\tau:V\times \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})\rightarrow \pi_{k-1}^{-1}(V)$.  Note that we can express $\tau$ as $(\pi_{k-1}(y),z')\mapsto s'(\pi_{k-1}(y))+z'$ for some continuous map $s':V\rightarrow \pi_{k-1}^{-1}(V)$.  The set $\varphi^{-1}(\pi_{k-1}^{-1}(V))$ is an open neighborhood of $x$. Take $U:=U^*\cap \pi_{k-1}(\varphi^{-1}(\pi^{-1}(V)))$ and note that the same homemorphism works replacing $U^*$ with $U$.

\[

We need to prove first that the topology of X/Z is textsclch and later we will use Lemma to prove that it is indeed an textsclch nilspace. Let pi_k-1:Xrightarrow X_k-1 be the usual quotient map in X. First we prove that the set C=\(x,x')in X^2: x=gx' for some gin Z\ is closed. Recall that $p$ is indeed a fibration (\cite[Proposition A.18]{CGSS-p-hom}), and note that $p_{k-1}:\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ is then a continuous fibration as well. Moreover $p_{k-1}$ is bijective. Indeed, for any elements $\pi_{k-1}(x),\pi_{k-1}(x')\in\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ such that $p_{k-1}(\pi_{k-1}(x))=p_{k-1}(\pi_{k-1}(x'))$, we have $\pi_{k-1}(p(x))=\pi_{k-1}(p(x'))$ and thus there exists a cube $\mathrm{c}\in \mathrm{C}^k(\mathrm{X})$ such that $\mathrm{c}(v)=p(x)$ for all $v\not=1^k$ and $\mathrm{c}(1^k)=p(x')$. Let $\mathrm{c}':\db{k}\rightarrow\mathrm{Y}$ be the map with $\mathrm{c}'(v)=x$ for all $v\not=1^k$ and $\mathrm{c}'(1^k)=x'$. Since $\mathrm{c}'$ restricted to $\db{k}\setminus\{1^k\}$ is a corner and $p$ is a fibration with $p\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}'|_{\db{k}\setminus\{1^k\}}=\mathrm{c}|_{\db{k}\setminus\{1^k\}}$, there exists $z\in \mathrm{Z}$ such that the map $\mathrm{c}'+1_{\{1^k\}}z$ is in $\mathrm{C}^k(\mathrm{Y})$. But note that $\mathrm{Z}^{\db{k}} = \mathrm{C}^k(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))$, so $1_{\{1^k\}}z\in \mathrm{C}^k(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))$, and therefore $\mathrm{c}'\in \mathrm{C}^k(\mathrm{Y})$. Hence $\pi_{k-1}(x)=\pi_{k-1}(x')$. By Theorem \ref{thm:open-mapping-general} the map $p_{k-1}$ is open, and therefore $p_{k-1}$ is an isomorphism of \textsc{lch} nilspaces. Hence every structure group of $\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ is a Lie group.

It therefore remains only to prove that the last structure group $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$ is also a Lie group. Recall from Proposition \ref{prop:k-th-group-action} that $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$ is isomorphic to any fixed fiber $F$ of $\pi_{k-1,\mathrm{Y}}$ where we fix some (any) element $e\in F$ to be the identity. Similarly, in $\mathrm{X}$ we fix the fiber $F':=p(F)$ and fix $p(e)$ as the zero element of $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$. The free action of $\mathrm{Z}$ on $F$ induces an inclusion of $\mathrm{Z}$ into $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$. The homormorphism $\phi_k:\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})\rightarrow\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$ can then be identified with $p|_F:F\rightarrow F'$. 

First we claim that the kernel of this homomorphism  $p|_F$ is precisely $e+\mathrm{Z}\subset F$. To see this, let $x\in F$ be any element such that $p(x)=p(e)$. By hypothesis on $p$, this means that if $\mathrm{c}\in F^{\db{k+1}}$ is the map $\mathrm{c}(v)=e$ for all $v\not=1^{k+1}$ and $\mathrm{c}(1^{k+1})=x$, there exists $d\in \mathrm{Z}^{\db{k+1}}$ such that $\mathrm{c}+d\in \mathrm{C}^{k+1}(\mathrm{Y})$. Note that we are not assuming that either $\mathrm{c}$ or $d$ are cubes for any nilspace, only that the sum $\mathrm{c}+d$ is. Then, by definition of the cubes in $\mathrm{C}^{k+1}(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))$ in terms of the single Gray-code linear equation, we can find a cube $d'\in \mathrm{C}^{k+1}(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))$ such that $d'(v)=-d(v)$ for all $v\not=1^{k+1}$. Hence $c+d+d'\in \mathrm{C}^{k+1}(\mathrm{Y})$. Note that all values of this cube are $e$ except perhaps the value at  $1^{k+1}$. By uniqueness of completion, this value must also be $e$. Hence $x+z=e$ for some $z\in \mathrm{Z}$,  which proves our claim.

Next, note that using the definition of addition in the fiber $F$ we have that the action of $\mathrm{Z}$ is also well defined and continuous. Furthermore, as mentioned above this free action induces an inclusion of $\mathrm{Z}$ in $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$, and $e+\mathrm{Z}$ is closed because it is precisely $p^{-1}(\{p(e)\})$.

Thus we have a short exact sequence $0\rightarrow \mathrm{Z} \rightarrow \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})\rightarrow 0$ where all groups are \textsc{lch} and $\mathrm{Z},\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$ are Lie. If $t\ge k$ then we can directly apply Proposition \ref{prop:ext-lie-is-lie-1} with $k=t$ (since $\mathrm{X},\mathrm{Y}$ are in particular $t$-step nilspaces).

For $t<k$, note that by \cite[Proposition A.18]{CGSS-p-hom} the nilspace $\mathrm{Y}$ is algebraically isomorphic to the fiber-product $\mathrm{Y}_t\times_{\mathrm{X}_t}\mathrm{X}$, with projection maps $p_t:\mathrm{Y}_t\rightarrow\mathrm{X}_t$ and $\pi_t:\mathrm{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}_t$. Note that the algebraic isomorphism is the map $\varphi(y)=(\pi_t(y),p(x))$, so here this is also a continuous map. Note that $p_t$ is also continuous, thus implying that $p_t$ is continuous as well because $p_t\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_{t,\mathrm{Y}} = \pi_{t,\mathrm{X}} \circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} p$. As $p$ is continuous and both $\pi_{t,\mathrm{Y}}$ and $\pi_{t,\mathrm{X}}$ are open and continuous we conclude that $p_t$ is continuous. By Proposition \ref{prop:ext-lie-is-lie-1} we get that $\mathrm{Y}_t$ is Lie-fibered as well, and $p_t$ is a continuous extension of $\mathrm{X}_t$. By Lemma \ref{lem:fib-prod-top-nil} we know that $\mathrm{Y}_t\times_{\mathrm{X}_t}\mathrm{X}$ is an \textsc{lch} nilspace. Hence, in order to prove that it is Lie-fibered, it suffices to prove that its structure groups are Lie groups.  The structure groups of $\mathrm{Y}_t\times_{\mathrm{X}_t}\mathrm{X}$ are easy to compute. Using the formula given in Lemma \ref{lem:fib-prod-top-nil} we deduce that for $i\le t$, the $i$-th structure group of $\mathrm{Y}_t\times_{\mathrm{X}_t}\mathrm{X}$ is $\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{Y}_t)$, which is Lie. For $i>t$ the $i$-th structure group of $\mathrm{Y}_t\times_{\mathrm{X}_t}\mathrm{X}$ is $\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{X})$ (which is Lie by assumption). Hence $\mathrm{Y}_t\times_{\mathrm{X}_t}\mathrm{X}$ is Lie-fibered. Then, Theorem \ref{thm:open-mapping-general} implies that the isomorphism  $\varphi$ is also a homeomorphism. Hence $\mathrm{Y}$ is Lie-fibered. The last sentence in the corollary follows from Theorem \ref{thm:open-mapping-thm}.

\label{def:fib-comp-cont}
Let $\mathrm{Y}$ be a nilspace endowed with an \textsc{lch} topology and let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step \textsc{lch} nilspace. Suppose that $\mathrm{Y}$ is a degree-$t$ algebraic nilspace extension of $\mathrm{X}$ by an abelian group $\mathrm{Z}$. Let $\Delta_{q:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}}:= \{(\mathrm{c}',\mathrm{c})\in \mathrm{Cor}^{t+1}(\mathrm{Y})\times \mathrm{C}^{t+1}(\mathrm{X}):q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}'(v)=\mathrm{c}(v)\text{ for all } v\not=1^{t+1}\}$. Let $\mathcal{K}_{(q)}:\Delta_{q:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}}\rightarrow \mathrm{Y}$ be the function that maps each $(\mathrm{c}',\mathrm{c})\in \Delta_{q:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}}$ to the unique element $y\in\mathrm{Y}$ which completes the corner $\mathrm{c}'$ and satisfies $q(y)=\mathrm{c}(1^{t+1})$. We argue by induction on $k$ (with $t$ fixed). For $k=1$ the result follows by Lemma \ref{lem:top-degree-k-k-ext}. 

For $k>1$, we prove that $\mathrm{Y}$ is an \textsc{lch} nilspace by proving that the conditions of Lemma \ref{lem:eq-def-lch-nil} are satisfied. Note that by $(i)$ the cube sets are closed, so we just need to prove that the completion functions are continuous. For $n>k$ this follows from $(ii)$. It then suffices to prove that $\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ is a degree-$t$ extension of $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ that satisfies all the assumptions in the theorem. Indeed, if we prove this, then by induction the completion functions on the factors of $\mathrm{Y}$ will also be continuous, as required in Lemma \ref{lem:eq-def-lch-nil}-$(ii)$. By Lemma \ref{lem:top-degree-k-k-ext} we can assume that $t<k$.

Recall that by \cite[Proposition A.19]{CGSS-p-hom} the following diagram commutes:
\begin{equation}\label{diag:factor-of-ext-1}
\begin{aligned}[c]
\begin{tikzpicture}
  \matrix (m) [matrix of math nodes,row sep=3em,column sep=4em,minimum width=2em]
  {\mathrm{Y} & \mathrm{X}  \\
     \mathrm{Y}_{k-1} & \mathrm{X}_{k-1}, \\};
  \path[-stealth]
    (m-1-1) edge node [above] {$q$} (m-1-2)
    (m-1-1) edge node [right] {$\pi$} (m-2-1)
    (m-1-2) edge node [right] {$\pi$} (m-2-2)
    (m-2-1) edge node [above] {$q_{k-1}$} (m-2-2);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

\vspace{-0.3cm}

\noindent where $q_{k-1}$ defines a degree-$t$ extension of $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$. (We just write $\pi$ instead of $\pi_{k-1}$ to avoid overloading the notation; the space where $\pi$ is defined will be clear from the context.)

Let us then prove that $\mathrm{Y}_{k-1},\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ satisfy all the  assumptions in the theorem.

Firstly, $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ with the quotient topology is an \textsc{lch} nilspace, by Theorem \ref{thm:factor-of-lch-nil} applied to $\mathrm{X}$.

Let us now analyze some properties of objects and maps in \eqref{diag:factor-of-ext-1}. The map $\pi:\mathrm{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ is open and continuous by Corollary \ref{cor:quotient-top-k-1-factor}. By Corollary \ref{cor:quotient-top-k-1-factor} applied to $\mathrm{Y}$,  the topology on $\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ is also \textsc{lch}. By Proposition \ref{prop:k-th-group-action} the $k$-th structure group $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$ is an \textsc{lch} topological group acting continuously on $\mathrm{Y}$. The group $\mathrm{Z}$ is an \textsc{lch} group by assumption. 

We claim that the action of $\mathrm{Z}$ on $\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ is continuous. This action is defined by the formula $\pi(y)+z:=\pi(y+z)$ (see \cite[Proposition A.19]{CGSS-p-hom}). To see that it is continuous, fix any sequences $(y_n)$ in $\mathrm{Y}$ and $(z_n)$ in $\mathrm{Z}$ such that $\pi(y_n)\rightarrow \pi(y)$ and $z_n\rightarrow z$. By Lemma \ref{lem:conv-quot} there exists a sequence $g_n\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$ such that $y_n+g_n\rightarrow y$. The continuity of the action of $\mathrm{Z}$ on $\mathrm{Y}$ implies  that $(y_n+g_n)+z_n\rightarrow y+z$. As $\pi$ is continuous, we know that $\pi((y_n+g_n)+z_n)\rightarrow \pi(y+z)=:\pi(y)+z$. We leave it as an exercise for the reader (using the uniqueness of completion on $\mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{Y})$) to see that $(y_n+g_n)+z_n=(y_n+z_n)+g_n$.  Then $\pi((y_n+g_n)+z_n)=\pi(y_n+z_n)=\pi(y_n)+z_n$, and the claimed continuity follows. This shows that Definition \ref{def:CtsAbBund}-$(iii)$ holds.

Next, note that since $q:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}$, $\pi:\mathrm{X}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ and $\pi:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ are open and continuous, we have that $q_{k-1}$ is open and continuous as well, by the commutativity of the diagram \eqref{diag:factor-of-ext-1}. This shows that Definition \ref{def:CtsAbBund}-$(iv)$ holds.

So far, we have proved that $q_{k-1}:\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ is a continuous $\mathrm{Z}$-bundle. We now prove that this bundle is also Cartan (i.e.\ the difference map is continuous). Suppose that $(\pi(y_n),\pi(y_n'))\rightarrow (\pi(y),\pi(y'))$ for some $(\pi(y_n),\pi(y_n'))$ and $ (\pi(y),\pi(y'))\in \mathrm{Y}_{k-1}\times_{\mathrm{X}_{k-1}}\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$. By Lemma \ref{lem:conv-quot} there are sequences $(g_n),(g_n')$ in $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$ such that $y_n+g_n\rightarrow y$ and $y_n'+g_n'\rightarrow y'$ in $\mathrm{Y}$. Hence, without loss of generality $y_n\rightarrow y$ and $y'_n\rightarrow y'$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. As $q_{k-1}(\pi(y_n))= q_{k-1}(\pi(y'_n))$, there exists $z_n\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$ such that $q(y_n)+z_n=q(y_n')$. As $\mathrm{X}$ is an \textsc{lch} nilspace, and $q$ is continuous, $z_n\rightarrow q(y)-q(y')=z\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. We leave it as an exercise for the reader to check that with the given assumptions (i.e.\ that $t<k$) the $k$-th structure homomorphism of $q$, $\phi_k:\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})\rightarrow \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$, is an (algebraic) group isomorphism (this follows from \cite[Definition 3.3.13]{Cand:Notes1} using the definition of cubes in an extension). To prove that $\phi_k$ is continuous, let $z_n'\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$ such that $z_n'\rightarrow z'$ as $n\rightarrow \infty$. Fix any $y_0\in \mathrm{Y}$. Then by definition $\phi_k(z_n')=q(y_0+z_n')-q(y_0)$. Since $\mathrm{Y}$ is Cartan, this is the composition of two continuous maps. Thus the limit is $q(y_0+z')-q(y_0)=\phi_k(z')$ as required. 
Hence, we have that $y_n+\phi_k^{-1}(z_n)\rightarrow y+\phi_k^{-1}(z)$ and $y_n'\rightarrow y'$. As $(y_n+\phi_k^{-1}(z_n),y_n')\in \mathrm{Y}\times_{\mathrm{X}}\mathrm{Y}$, by continuity of the difference map in $\mathrm{Y}$ we have $(y_n+\phi_k^{-1}(z_n))-y_n'\rightarrow (y+\phi_k^{-1}(z))-y'$.\footnote{Note that in this last equation the ``$+$'' signs denote addition of an element of $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$ and the ``$-$'' signs denote difference of two points that give an element in the extension group $\mathrm{Z}$.} This confirms  that the difference map $\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}\times_{\mathrm{X}_{k-1}}\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ is continuous. 

It remains to check that $\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ satisfies properties $(i)$, $(ii)$, $(iii)$ in the theorem.

Property $(i)$ follows from Lemma \ref{lem:closure-cube-in-k-1-factor} applied to $\mathrm{Y}$.

Let us now prove $(ii)$, i.e.\ that completion on $\mathrm{Cor}^k(\mathrm{Y}_{k-1})$ is continuous. By continuity of $q$, we have $q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n)\rightarrow q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}'$ in $\mathrm{Cor}^k(\mathrm{X})$. Now we argue by a diagonalization, as follows. For every $m\in \mathbb{N}$, let $B_{1/m}(q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c})\subset \mathrm{C}^k(\mathrm{X})$ be the open ball of radius $1/m$ and center $q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}$. Note that for this step to work it is crucial that $t<k$, as we are precisely applying the fiber-completion function to faces of dimension $t+1$ inside $\db{k}$. The process is as follows: first, for every $n\ge 1$ choose an element $f_n\in\mathrm{C}^k(\mathcal{D}_t(\mathrm{Z}))$ such that $(\mathrm{c}_n+f_n)(v) =(\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n)(v)$ for $v\in \db{k}_{\le t}$. Then, the continuity of the fiber-completion implies that $(\mathrm{c}_n+f_n)(1^k)$ converges to the unique completion of $(\mathrm{c}',q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c})$. We first claim that T is a Cartan continuous Z_k-bundle over X. To see that $(ii)$ holds, note that for any corner $(\mathrm{c}_0',\mathrm{c}_1')\in \mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathcal{T})$, its completion is just $(\mathcal{K}_{k+1}(\mathrm{c}_0'),\mathcal{K}_{k+1}(\mathrm{c}_1'))$, where $\mathcal{K}_{k+1}$ is the completion function on $\mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X})$.

For $k=1$, since  $\alpha$ then just adds a constant, it is  indeed a translation on $\mathcal{D}_1(A_1)$. Now we prove that every translation $\alpha\in \Theta_s(\mathrm{X})$ has the form claimed in the theorem. Note that by the previous paragraph, adding a constant $x_i$ in the $i$-th component of $\mathrm{X}$ is a translation in $\Theta_i(\mathrm{X})$. Moreover, for $i\geq k-s+1$ such translations are central in $\Theta_s(\mathrm{X})$. Hence for every $x\in \mathrm{X}$ we have $\alpha(x)=\alpha(x_1,\ldots,x_{k-s},0^s)+(0^{k-s},x_{k-s+1},\ldots,x_k)$. On the other hand, by the above expression of $\alpha$, this map equals $\langle\mathrm{c}^*,\mathrm{c}^*\rangle_s+\langle0,\mathrm{c}'\rangle_s+\langle 0,\mathrm{c}''\rangle_s$ for some $\mathrm{c}'=(\mathrm{c}'_1,\ldots,\mathrm{c}'_{k-s},0^s)\in \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$, and with $\mathrm{c}''(v)=(0^{k-s},g'\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}(v))$. We argue by induction on the step $k$. For $k=1$, the nilspace $\mathrm{X}$ is topologically isomorphic to $\mathcal{D}_1(\mathrm{Z})$ where $\mathrm{Z}$ is an abelian Lie group. By known results (see e.g.\ \cite[Theorem 2.4]{Mosk}) we have $\mathrm{Z}\cong \mathbb{R}^m\times \mathbb{T}^n\times D$ for some discrete abelian group $D$. By \cite[Corollary 12]{Fu&Shak}, if $\mathrm{Z}$ is compactly generated then $D$ is finitely generated, hence of the form $\mathbb{Z}^r\times G$ for some finite abelian group $G$. The conclusion of the theorem then clearly holds in this case.

Let $k>1$ and suppose by induction that $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ satisfies the desired conclusion, so there is a $(k-1)$-step free nilspace $F_{k-1}$, and a fibration $\varphi_{k-1}: F_{k-1}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}_{k-1}$. We then define the fiber-product
$\mathrm{Y}:=F_{k-1}\times_{\mathrm{X}_{k-1}}\mathrm{X} = \{(f,x)\in F_{k-1}\times \mathrm{X}: \varphi_{k-1}(f)=\pi_{k-1}(x)\}$. Algebraically this is a $k$-step nilspace that is a degree-$k$ extension of $F$ by the structure group $\mathrm{Z}_k=\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$ (see \cite[Proposition A.17]{CGSS-p-hom}). In particular (using for instance \cite[Proposition A.21]{CGSS-p-hom}) for each $i\in [k-1]$ the $i$-th nilspace factor $\pi_i(\mathrm{Y})$ is isomorphic to the $i$-th nilspace factor $F_i$ of $F_{k-1}$. Recall also that $\pi_{k-1,\mathrm{Y}}$ is just projection to the $F_{k-1}$ component. By Lemma \ref{lem:fib-prod-top-nil} we also know that $\mathrm{Y}$ is a Lie-fibered nilspace. It is straightforwardly seen that the component projections $p_1:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow F_{k-1}$, $(f,x)\mapsto f$ and $p_2:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}$, $(f,x)\mapsto x$ are continuous fibrations. By Theorem \ref{thm:splitext}, the nilspace $\mathrm{Y}$ is a  split extension, so $\mathrm{Y}\cong F_{k-1}\times \mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k)$. $C:=\{\alpha\in \Theta(F):\forall x,y\in \mathrm{X}, \text{ if } \varphi(x)=\varphi(y) \text{ then } \varphi(\alpha(x))=\varphi(\alpha(y))\}$. Note that $C$ is a closed subgroup of $\Theta(F)$. Hence $C$ is a Lie group (by Theorem \ref{thm:freetransLie} and Cartan's theorem). Let $\widehat{\varphi}:C\rightarrow \Theta(\mathrm{X})$ be the homomorphism induced by $\varphi$ as in \cite[Lemma 1.5]{CGSS}. 
 To see that $\widehat{\varphi}$ is continuous, let $\alpha_n\rightarrow\alpha$ in $\Theta(F)$, that is, for any compact set $K\subset F$ we have $\sup_{s\in K}d_{F}(\alpha_n(s),\alpha(s))\rightarrow 0$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. We need to check that for every compact set $K'\subset \mathrm{X}$ we have $\sup_{x\in K'}d_{\mathrm{X}}(\widehat{\varphi}(\alpha_n)(x),\widehat{\varphi}(\alpha)(x))\rightarrow 0$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. By Corollary \ref{cor:cpct-sets-are-im-of-cpct-sets}, there exists a compact set $K\subset F$ such that $\varphi(K)=K'$. Suppose for a contradiction that $\sup_{x\in K'}d_{\mathrm{X}}(\widehat{\varphi}(\alpha_n)(x),\widehat{\varphi}(\alpha)(x))\not\rightarrow 0$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. Then, passing to a subsequence if necessary, we can assume that for some $\epsilon>0$ we have  $\sup_{x\in K'}d_{\mathrm{X}}(\widehat{\varphi}(\alpha_n)(x),\widehat{\varphi}(\alpha)(x))>\epsilon$ for all $n$. In particular, there exists a sequence $x_n\in K'$ such that $d_{\mathrm{X}}(\widehat{\varphi}(\alpha_n)(x_n),\widehat{\varphi}(\alpha)(x_n))>\epsilon$ for all $n$. For each $n$ let $s_n\in K$ be any element such that $\varphi(s_n)=x_n$. By compactness of $K'$ we can assume that $s_n\rightarrow s\in K$ as $n\rightarrow \infty$. This yields a contradiction, because $d_{\mathrm{X}}(\varphi(\alpha_n(s_n)),\varphi(\alpha(s_n)))=d_{\mathrm{X}}(\widehat{\varphi}(\alpha_n)(x_n),\widehat{\varphi}(\alpha)(x_n))>\epsilon$, whereas $\alpha_n(s_n))\rightarrow \alpha(s)$ and $\alpha(s_n))\rightarrow\alpha(s)$ as $n\rightarrow \infty$. An orbit relation of a subgroup of $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ is not necessarily a congruence. For instance, let $\mathrm{X}:=\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{Z}_2)\times \mathcal{D}_2(\mathbb{Z}_2)$ and $\alpha\in \Theta(\mathrm{X})$ be the map $(x,y)\mapsto (x,x+y)$ (this is a translation by Theorem \ref{thm:decrip-trans-group}). To prove this, consider the cubes $\mathrm{c}_1,\mathrm{c}_2\in \mathrm{C}^3(\mathrm{X})$ defined as $\mathrm{c}_1(v_1,v_2,v_3)=(1-v_3,0)$ and $\mathrm{c}_2(v_1,v_2,v_3)= (v_3,v_1v_2)$. Note that the cubes $\pi_\sim \circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_1 $ and $\pi_\sim \circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_2$ are adjacent (see \cite[Definition 3.1.6]{Cand:Notes1}) in the sense that $\pi_\sim \circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_1(v_1,v_2,0)= \pi_\sim \circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_2(v_1,v_2,1)$. Thus, by \cite[Lemma 3.1.7]{Cand:Notes1} we have that the function $\mathrm{c}_3\in (\pi_\sim(\mathrm{X}))^{\db{3}}$ defined as $\mathrm{c}_3(v_1,v_2,v_3):=\pi_\sim(0,0)$ for $(v_1,v_2,v_3)\not=(1,1,0)$ and $\mathrm{c}_3(1,1,0)=\pi_\sim(0,1)$ should be in $\mathrm{C}^3(\pi_\sim(\mathrm{X})):=\{\pi_\sim \circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}:\mathrm{c}\in \mathrm{C}^3(\mathrm{X})\}$. It can be checked that $\mathrm{c}_3$ does not equal $\pi_\sim\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}$ for any $\mathrm{c}\in \mathrm{C}^3(\mathrm{X})$. \label{rem:cosnilex}
Important (and particularly simple) examples of nilspaces that arise as quotients by groupable congruences are \emph{coset nilspaces}. Recall (e.g.\ from  \cite[Proposition 2.3.1]{Cand:Notes1}) that a $k$-step coset nilspace $\mathrm{X}$ is constructed starting with a filtered group $(G,G_\bullet)$ of degree $k$ and a subgroup $\Gamma\subset G$, and letting $\mathrm{X}$ be the set $G/\Gamma = \pi_\Gamma(G)$ of left cosets of $\Gamma$ in $G$ equipped with the cube sets $\pi_\Gamma^{\db{n}}(\mathrm{C}^n(G_\bullet))$, $n\geq 0$. Then the orbit relation $\sim_\Gamma$ (where elements of $\Gamma$ act by right-multiplication on $G$) is a groupable congruence on the \emph{group nilspace}  $\widetilde{\mathrm{X}}$ associated with $(G,G_\bullet)$. Indeed if $g,g'\in G$ satisfy $g'= g\gamma$ for some $\gamma\in \Gamma$ and $g G_{i+1} = g' G_{i+1}$ (i.e.\ $\pi_i(g)=\pi_i(g')$ in the group nilspace), then clearly $\gamma\in G_{i+1}$, so the translation on $\widetilde{\mathrm{X}}$ consisting in right-multiplication by $\gamma$ is already in $\Theta_{i+1}(\widetilde{\mathrm{X}})$, and therefore \eqref{eq:groupable} holds. In Section \ref{sec:DC} we shall see a more general example of groupable congruences, involving \emph{double}-coset spaces.

\label{rem:congfibr}
The following example shows that not all cube-surjective morphisms are fibrations, thus confirming the fact mentioned earlier, that not every congruence induces a fibration.
Let $\mathrm{X}=\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{Z}_2)\times \mathcal{D}_2(\mathbb{Z}_2)$, and let $\mathbb{F}_2^\omega=\bigoplus_{n=1}^\infty \mathbb{F}_2$. It can be proved that there exists a map $f:\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{F}_2^\omega)\rightarrow \mathrm{X}$ that is arbitrarily well-balanced, meaning that for every $b>0$ there exists $N_b>0$ such that for any $n\ge N_b$ the map $f_n:\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{F}_2^n)\rightarrow \mathrm{X}$, $v\mapsto f(v\times 0^{\mathbb{N}\setminus [n]})$ is $b$-balanced in the sense of  \cite[Definition 5.1]{CSinverse} (this is a non-trivial fact about nilspaces, but we omit the details in this paper as we will avoid such examples).

Let $\sim$ be the equivalence induced by $f$, i.e.\ for $x,y\in \mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{F}_2^\omega)$ we have $x\sim y$ $\Leftrightarrow$ $f(x)=f(y)$. Then $\sim$ is a nilspace congruence and $\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{F}_2^\omega)/\!\!\sim$ is isomorphic to the nilspace $\mathrm{X}$. Indeed, first note that the map $f_\sim:\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{F}_2^\omega)/\!\!\sim\, \rightarrow \mathrm{X}$, $\pi_\sim(x) \mapsto f(x)$ is well-defined and injective. We claim that for all $n\ge 0$ the map $f^{\db{n}}:\mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{F}_2^\omega))\rightarrow \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ is surjective (hence in particular $f_\sim$ is surjective, hence bijective). Let us denote by $i_n:\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{F}_2^n)\rightarrow \mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{F}_2^\omega)$ the usual inclusion. As $\mathrm{X}$ is finite, so is $\mathrm{C}^m(\mathrm{X})$ for any $m\ge 0$. The Haar probability measure $\mu_{\mathrm{C}^m(\mathrm{X})}$ is then the normalized counting measure. Fixing any $\mathrm{c}\in\mathrm{C}^m(\mathrm{X})$, we therefore have $\mu_{\mathrm{C}^m(\mathrm{X})}(\{\mathrm{c}\})\gg_{m} 1$. Then, by definition of balance, there is $N_{\mathrm{c}}>0$ such that for $n\geq N_{\mathrm{c}}$ the pushforward measure $\nu:=\mu_{\mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{F}_2^n))}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (f\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} i_n)^{-1}$ is sufficiently close to $\mu_{\mathrm{C}^m(\mathrm{X})}$ in the vague topology to be able to conclude that $\nu(\{\mathrm{c}\})>0$, which implies the claimed surjectivity of $f^{\db{n}}$. Now note that $f_\sim:\pi_\sim(x)\mapsto f(x)$ is a nilspace a morphism, and its inverse is a morphism as well, because for any $\mathrm{c}\in \mathrm{C}^m(\mathrm{X})$, by the cube-surjectivity we know that there exists $\mathrm{c}^*\in \mathrm{C}^m(\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{F}_2^\omega))$ such that $f\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}^*=\mathrm{c}$. But $f$ factors through $\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{F}_2^\omega)/\sim$, $f=f_\sim \circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_\sim$ and as $f_\sim$ is a bijection we have that $f_\sim^{-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c} = \pi_\sim \circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}^*\in \mathrm{C}^m(\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{F}_2^\omega)/\sim)$. We have thus proved that $f$ is a cube-surjective morphism. However $f$ cannot be a fibration, because the image nilspace of a fibration is always of step at most as large as the step of its domain nilspace, and here  $\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{F}_2^\omega)$ is 1-step whereas $\mathrm{X}$ is 2-step.

nodes.statement: Another seemingly natural condition on H_bullet that one could have tried to use instead of Definition is to require just that each subgroup H_i is closed in Theta(X). However, this leaves open the possibility that at the level of some lower-step factor of X a failure of closure occurs, making the quotient of X by sim_H non-viable topologically because some of its factors are not Hausdorff. Indeed, for example, let X be the group nilspace R with the 2-step filtration R=Rge Zge \0\. Let Hsubset Theta(X) be the subgroup of translations \ xmapsto x+sqrt2n: ninZ\. Clearly H is a discrete subgroup, hence closed. Moreover, no translation in H is in Theta_2(X)congZ, so H_2=\id\ and is therefore also closed. However, the 1-step factor of X is X_1 = R/Z, and eta_1(H) acts on X_1 as the group \sqrt2n\!\!mod 1:nin Z\, a non-closed subgroup of Theta_1(X_1) = R/Z. Thus, the quotient X/H (which algebraically is a perfectly valid quotient nilspace) has 1-step factor the group sqrt2Zbackslash (R/Z)cong R/(Z+sqrt2Z), which is not Hausdorff.

However, this leaves open the possibility that at the level of some lower-step factor of $\mathrm{X}$ a failure of closure occurs, making the quotient of $\mathrm{X}$ by $\sim_H$ non-viable topologically because some of its factors are not Hausdorff. Indeed, for example, let $\mathrm{X}$ be the group nilspace $\mathbb{R}$ with the 2-step filtration $\mathbb{R}=\mathbb{R}\ge \mathbb{Z}\ge \{0\}$. Let $H\subset \Theta(\mathrm{X})$ be the subgroup of translations $\{ x\mapsto x+\sqrt{2}n: n\in\mathbb{Z}\}$. Clearly $H$ is a discrete subgroup, hence closed. Moreover, no translation in $H$ is in $\Theta_2(\mathrm{X})\cong\mathbb{Z}$, so $H_2=\{\mathrm{id}\}$ and is therefore also closed. However, the 1-step factor of $\mathrm{X}$ is $\mathrm{X}_1 = \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$, and $\eta_1(H)$ acts on $\mathrm{X}_1$ as the group $\{\sqrt{2}n\!\!\mod 1:n\in \mathbb{Z}\}$, a non-closed subgroup of $\Theta_1(\mathrm{X}_1) = \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$. Thus, the quotient $\mathrm{X}/H$ (which algebraically is a perfectly valid quotient nilspace) has 1-step factor the group $\sqrt{2}\mathbb{Z}\backslash (\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z})\cong  \mathbb{R}/(\mathbb{Z}+\sqrt{2}\mathbb{Z})$, which is not Hausdorff.

\label{prop:quot-lcfr-nil}
Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step Lie-fibered nilspace and let $H_\bullet$ be a closed fiber-transitive filtration on $\mathrm{X}$. Then $\pi_H(\mathrm{X})$ equipped with the quotient topology is an \textsc{lch} space.

nodes.statement: Since pi_H(X) is the quotient of an textsclch space by the action of a group of homeomorphisms, the map pi_H is continuous and open. Hence pi_H(X) is second-countable, and it is also locally compact . To prove that pi_H(X) is Hausdorff it suffices to show that the set C=\(x,y)inX^2:xsim_H y\ is closed in the product topology . Since X is textsclch, it is metrizable , so closure in X is equivalent to sequential closure. Let ((x_n,h_n x_n))_n be a sequence in C convergent to (x,y)in X^2. By Lemma there is a convergent sequence (h_n')_n in H with limit hin H such that h_nx_n=h_n'x_n for all n. Since x_nrightarrow x, the continuity of the action implies h_n' x_nrightarrow hx, so y=hx and C is closed.
nodes.raw_latex: Since $\pi_H(\mathrm{X})$ is the quotient of an \textsc{lch} space by the action of a group of homeomorphisms, the map $\pi_H$ is continuous and open. Hence $\pi_H(\mathrm{X})$ is second-countable, and it is also locally compact \cite[Ex.\ 29.3]{Mu}. To prove that $\pi_H(\mathrm{X})$ is Hausdorff it suffices to show that the set $C=\{(x,y)\in\mathrm{X}^2:x\sim_H y\}$ is closed in the product topology \cite[p.\ 79, Prop.\ 8]{BourbakiGT1}. Since $\mathrm{X}$ is \textsc{lch}, it is metrizable \cite[Ex.\ 32.3 and Thm.\ 34.1]{Mu}, so closure in $\mathrm{X}$ is equivalent to sequential closure. Let $((x_n,h_n x_n))_n$ be a sequence in $C$ convergent to $(x,y)\in \mathrm{X}^2$. By Lemma \ref{lem:re-param-conv-seq} there is a convergent sequence $(h_n')_n$ in $H$ with limit $h\in H$ such that $h_nx_n=h_n'x_n$ for all $n$. Since $x_n\rightarrow x$, the continuity of the action implies $h_n' x_n\rightarrow hx$, so $y=hx$ and $C$ is closed.

nodes.statement: Let Z be a Polish abelian group and let H be a closed subgroup of Z. Then for all integers nge 0 and kge 1 the following holds: for every convergent sequence (g_m)_min N in C^n(D_k(Z))+H^dbn (in the product topology on Z^dbn), there exist convergent sequences (c_m)_m in C^n(D_k(Z)) and (d_m)_m in H^dbn such that c_m+d_m=g_m for all m. In particular, the group C^n(D_k(Z))+H^dbn is a closed subgroup of Z^dbn.

\label{lem:closure-sum-of-cu-and-h}
Let $\mathrm{Z}$ be a Polish abelian group and let $H$ be a closed subgroup of $\mathrm{Z}$. Then for all integers $n\ge 0$ and $k\ge 1$ the following holds: for every convergent sequence $(g_m)_{m\in \mathbb{N}}$ in $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))+H^{\db{n}}$ (in the product topology on $\mathrm{Z}^{\db{n}}$), there exist convergent sequences $(\mathrm{c}_m)_m$ in $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))$ and $(d_m)_m$ in $H^{\db{n}}$ such that $\mathrm{c}_m+d_m=g_m$ for all $m$. In particular, the group $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))+H^{\db{n}}$ is a closed subgroup of $\mathrm{Z}^{\db{n}}$.

Let $(g_m)_m$ be a convergent sequence in $\mathrm{C}^{k+1}(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))+H^{\db{k+1}}$. Let us define $\mathrm{c}_m'\in \mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))$ as $\mathrm{c}_m':=g_m|_{\db{k+1}\setminus\{1^{k+1}\}}$ (note that $\mathrm{c}_m'$ is indeed in $\mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))$ since any map $\db{k}\rightarrow \mathrm{Z}$ is in $\mathrm{C}^k(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))$). As $(g_m)$ is convergent, so is $(\mathrm{c}_m')$. For every $m$ let $\mathrm{c}_m^*\in \mathrm{C}^{k+1}(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))$ be the unique completion of $\mathrm{c}_m'$. By continuity of the completion function,  the sequence $(\mathrm{c}_m^*)$ converges to a limit in $\mathrm{C}^{k+1}(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))$ (equal to the completion of the limit of $(\mathrm{c}_m')$). Finally, let us define $f_m:=g_m-\mathrm{c}_m^*\in \mathrm{Z}^{\db{k+1}}$. As a pointwise difference of two convergent sequences, the sequence $(f_m)$ converges. We now prove that $f_m\in H^{\db{k+1}}$ for every $m$, which will complete the proof in this case (since $H$ is closed). First note that clearly $f_m\sbr{v}=0$ for all $v\not=1^{k+1}$ so it suffices to prove that $f_m(1^{k+1})\in H$. Recall from  \cite[Definition 2.2.22]{Cand:Notes1} the Gray-code map $\sigma_{k+1}:\mathrm{Z}^{\db{k+1}}\rightarrow\mathrm{Z}$, $r\mapsto \sum_{v\in \db{k+1}} (-1)^{|v|}r\sbr{v}$, where $|v|:=v\sbr{1}+\cdots+v\sbr{k+1}$. The map $\pi_H^{\db{n}}:\mathrm{X}^{\db{n}}\rightarrow (\pi_H(\mathrm{X}))^{\db{n}}$ is open, so to prove the closure of $\mathrm{C}^n(\pi_H(\mathrm{X}))$ it suffices to prove that $(\pi_H^{\db{n}})^{-1}\mathrm{C}^n(\pi_H(\mathrm{X}))=H^{\db{n}} \cdot \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ is closed. Note that it suffices to prove that if $(g_m)$ is a convergent sequence in $H^{\db{n}}\cdot \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ then there exist convergent sequences $(d_m')$ in $H^{\db{n}}$ and $(\mathrm{c}_m')$ in $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ such that $d_m'\cdot \mathrm{c}_m' = g_m$ for all $m$. We prove this by induction on $k$, the case $k=0$ being trivial. 

For $k>0$, we first prove that $H^{\db{n}} \cdot \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ is (algebraically) an abelian bundle over $\eta_{k-1}(H)^{\db{n}} \cdot \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ with structure group $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k))+H_k^{\db{n}}$, where $\mathrm{Z}_k=\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$.

For $n\le k$ note that the claimed structure group $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k))+H_k^{\db{n}}$ is simply $\mathrm{Z}_k^{\db{n}}$. But if $d\cdot \mathrm{c}, d'\cdot \mathrm{c}'\in  H^{\db{n}} \cdot\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ have the same image under $\pi_{k-1}^{\db{n}}$ then they indeed differ in an element $f\in \mathrm{Z}_k^{\db{n}}$ by definition, so our claim holds.

For $n= k+1$, suppose again that $d\cdot \mathrm{c}, d'\cdot \mathrm{c}'\in H^{\db{n}}\cdot \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ are equal modulo $\pi_{k-1}^{\db{n}}$. For each $v\in \db{k+1}\setminus\{1^{k+1}\}$, let $f(v)\in \mathrm{Z}_k$ be the unique element such that $(d\cdot \mathrm{c})(v)+f(v)=(d'\cdot\mathrm{c}')(v)$. By uniqueness of $(k+1)$-corner completion on $\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k)$, the map $f$ extends uniquely to an element $f\in \mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k))$. Since the action of $\mathrm{Z}_k$ commutes with translations, we can assume  (renaming $\mathrm{c}+f$ as $\mathrm{c}$) that $d\cdot \mathrm{c}(v)=d' \cdot \mathrm{c}'(v)$ for every $v\neq 1^{k+1}$, and $\pi_{k-1}(d\cdot \mathrm{c}(1^{k+1}))=\pi_{k-1}(d' \cdot \mathrm{c}'(1^{k+1}))$. Hence there is $z\in \mathrm{Z}_k$ such that $(d\cdot \mathrm{c})(1^{k+1})=(d'\cdot \mathrm{c}')(1^{k+1})+z$. We claim that $z\in H_k$. Let us denote by $\mathrm{c}_z\in \mathrm{Z}_k^{\db{k+1}}$ the map that equals $z$ at  $1^{k+1}$ and 0 elsewhere. Then $\mathrm{c}+\mathrm{c}_z=d^{-1}d'\cdot \mathrm{c}'$, and we want to deduce that $z\in H_k$. Note that $(d^{-1}d'\cdot \mathrm{c}')|_{\db{k+1}\setminus\{1^{k+1}\}} = \mathrm{c}|_{\db{k+1}\setminus\{1^{k+1}\}}$, so this is in $\mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X})$. By the last sentence of Lemma \ref{lem:cong-equi}, there exists $d^*\in \mathrm{C}^{k+1}(H_\bullet)$ such that $(d^{-1}d'\cdot \mathrm{c}')|_{\db{k+1}\setminus\{1^{k+1}\}} = (d^*\cdot \mathrm{c}')|_{\db{k+1}\setminus\{1^{k+1}\}}$. Let $\gamma:=(d^{-1}d'(d^*)^{-1})(1^{k+1})\in H$, and let $d_\gamma\in H^{\db{k+1}}$ be the map with $d_\gamma(1^{k+1})=\gamma$ and $d_\gamma(v)=\mathrm{id}_H$ otherwise. Then $d^{-1}d'\cdot \mathrm{c}' = d_\gamma d^*\cdot \mathrm{c}'$.  Hence $\mathrm{c}+\mathrm{c}_z = d_\gamma d^*\cdot \mathrm{c}'$. But $\mathrm{c}$ and $d^*\cdot \mathrm{c}'$ are elements of $\mathrm{C}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X})$ that are equal when restricted to $\db{k+1}\setminus\{1^{k+1}\}$. By uniqueness of completion we then have $\mathrm{c}(1^{k+1})+z= \gamma(d^*\cdot\mathrm{c}'(1^{k+1})) = \gamma(\mathrm{c}(1^{k+1}))$. By property \eqref{eq:ft-fil}, this implies that $z\in H_k$.

Now let $(d_m\cdot \mathrm{c}_m)$ be a convergent sequence in $H^{\db{n}}\cdot \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$. This implies that the sequence $(\eta_{k-1}(d_m)\cdot \pi_{k-1}(\mathrm{c}_m))$ converges in $\eta_{k-1}(H)^{\db{n}}\cdot \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$. By induction, there exist $d_m'\in H^{\db{n}}$ and $\mathrm{c}_m'\in \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ such that the sequence  $\eta_{k-1}(d_m')$ converges in $\eta_{k-1}(H)^{\db{n}}$, $(\pi_{k-1}(\mathrm{c}_m'))$ converges in $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$, and $\eta_{k-1}(d_m')\pi_{k-1}(\mathrm{c}_m')=\eta_{k-1}(d_m)\cdot \pi_{k-1}(\mathrm{c}_m)$. By Lemma \ref{lem:conv-polish-group} we can assume that $d_m'$ converges in $H^{\db{n}}$ and by Lemma \ref{lem:open-projection-of-cubes} we can assume that $\mathrm{c}_m'$ converges in $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ as well. Since $d_m'\cdot \mathrm{c}_m'$ is an element of $H^{\db{n}}\cdot \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ equal to $d_m\cdot \mathrm{c}_m$ modulo $\pi_{k-1}$, by the previous paragraph  we have $d_m'\cdot \mathrm{c}_m'-d_m\cdot \mathrm{c}_m\in \mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k))+H_k^{\db{n}}$. As both $(d_m'\cdot \mathrm{c}_m')$ and $(d_m\cdot \mathrm{c}_m)$ converge, so does $(d_m'\cdot \mathrm{c}_m'-d_m\cdot \mathrm{c}_m)$. Moreover, by Lemma \ref{lem:closure-sum-of-cu-and-h} there exist convergent sequences $(f_m)$ in $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k))$ and $(\gamma_m)$ in $H_k^{\db{n}}$ such that $d_m'\cdot \mathrm{c}_m'-d_m\cdot \mathrm{c}_m=f_m+\gamma_m$. In particular $d_m\cdot \mathrm{c}_m = d_m'\cdot\mathrm{c}_m'-f_m-d_m = (d_m'-\gamma_m)\cdot (\mathrm{c}_m'-f_m)$. But $(\mathrm{c}_m'-f_m)$ is a convergent sequence in the closed set $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$, with limit $\mathrm{c}$ say, and so is  $(d_m'-\gamma_m)$ in $H^{\db{n}}$, with limit $d$, so $d_m\cdot \mathrm{c}_m$ converges to $d\cdot \mathrm{c}\in H^{\db{n}}\cdot \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$, which proves the claimed closure.

It suffices to prove continuity $\mathcal{K}_{k+1}$ on $\pi_H(\mathrm{X})$. Indeed, then the same result applied with $k=n$ will yield the continuity of completion of $\mathcal{K}_{n+1}$ on $\pi_{\eta_{n}(H)}(\mathrm{X}_{n})$, for any $n\le k$, when considering $\pi_{\eta_{n}(H)}(\mathrm{X}_{n})$ as the quotient of $\mathrm{X}_n$ modulo the congruence  induced by $\eta_n(H)$ (with the quotient topology). nodes.raw_latex:
\label{lem:cont-diff-map-coset}
Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step Lie-fibered nilspace, with $k$-th structure group $\mathrm{Z}_k$, and let $H_\bullet$ be a closed fiber-transitive filtration on $\mathrm{X}$. Then $\pi_H(\mathrm{X})$ is a Cartan principal $\mathrm{Z}_k/H_k$-bundle over $\pi_{k-1}(\pi_H(\mathrm{X}))$.

nodes.statement: One may naturally wonder to what extent the closure property in Definition is necessary to ensure that the quotient of X by sim_H is a Lie-fibered nilspace. It turns out that for X a free nilspace, a variant condition can be proved to be necessary and sufficient. More precisely, if F is a k-step free nilspace and H is a fiber-transitive group on F, it can be proved that pi_H(F) is a Lie-fibered nilspace if and only if for every iin [k] the group eta_i(complH) is a closed subgroup of Theta(F_i). We shall not need this fact in this paper, so let us just outline the argument here. First one proves that more generally if H is a fiber-transitive group on a Lie-fibered nilspace, then complH=ker(widehatpi_H) and so complH must be a closed subgroup of Theta(F). Then, the same fact applied on F_i implies that completa_i(H) is closed in Theta(F_i). This yields the necessity of the above condition. Then, using that F is a free nilspace, the additional property that for every iin [k] we obtain the additional fact that eta_i(complH)=completa_i(H), and this implies the sufficiency of the above condition (indeed we then need not ask for all the terms in the filtration of complH to be closed, because the filtration is (complHcap Theta_i(F))_iin[k], and similarly for lower steps. Hence, as Theta_i(F) is always closed, it suffices to require complH to be closed, and for lower-step factors it suffices to require eta_i(complH) to be closed).

Given any such metric $d$ on $\mathrm{X}$, we can define a metric $d'$ on $\pi_H(F)$ simply by declaring $d'(x,y):=d(\varphi(x),\varphi(y))$. As $\varphi$ is a homeomorphism onto its image this is indeed a metric on $\pi_H(F)$. Relative to $d'$ and $d$, the map $\varphi$ is an isometry.

\label{rem:2-step-embed}
Corollary \ref{cor:k=2-str-good}  and Proposition \ref{prop:embeb-strong-good} together imply that  any 2-step \textsc{cfr} nilspace can be embedded into a coset nilspace corresponding to a 2-step connected nilmanifold. This will enable us to recover and extend a recent inverse theorem of Jamneshan and Tao \cite{J&T} for the Gowers $U^3$-norm on finite abelian groups; see Theorem \ref{thm:jam-tao}. Note that a version of the above embedding result was proved  for finite 2-step nilspaces by Host and Kra in \cite[Theorem 3]{HK-par}.

\label{lem:closed-group-as-trans}
Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a group nilspace associated with a filtered Lie group of finite degree $(G,G_\bullet)$. Let $\tau:G\rightarrow \Theta(\mathrm{X})$ be the injective homomorphism $g\mapsto \tau_g$ where $\tau_g(s):=gs$. Then for any closed subgroup $H$ of $G$, we have that $\tau(H)$ is a closed subgroup of $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$.

nodes.statement: That Kbackslash G/Gamma is algebraically a (double-coset) nilspace follows from the assumption that (K,Gamma) is a groupable nilpair. We claim that the fiber-transitive filtration (K_i:=Kcap G_i)_igeq 0 is closed on G. Indeed, by Lemma , for each i the group KG_i+1/G_i+1 acting by left-multiplication on G/G_i+1 is a closed subgroup of Theta(G/G_i+1) (since KG_i+1/G_i+1 is closed in G/G_i+1). Moreover, using the identity eta_i(K_j)=(Kcap G_j)G_i+1/G_i+1= (KG_i+1/G_i+1) cap (G_j G_i+1/G_i+1), we have that for all iin[k], the closure of KG_i+1/G_i+1 implies that for all i,jin[k] the subgroup eta_i(Kcap G_j) is closed. This proves our claim. Applying Theorem to the group nilspace (G,G_bullet) and the closed fiber-transitive filtration (K_i)_igeq 0 we get that Kbackslash G is a k-step Lie-fibered nilspace. Applying Theorem again but now to the action of Gamma by right multiplication on Kbackslash G (noting that the assumptions imply that this defines a closed groupable congruence), the result follows.

By Theorem \ref{thm:groupequivrep} there is a free nilspace $F$ and a  fiber-transitive group $\Gamma\subset \Theta(F)$ which is fiber-discrete and  fiber-cocompact, such that $\pi_\Gamma(F)\cong \mathrm{X}$. Let $G=\Theta(F)$, which is a Lie group by Corollary \ref{cor:trans&structFree}, and let $G_\bullet$ be the filtration $(G_i:=\Theta_i(F))_{i\geq 0}$. Let $\Gamma_\bullet$ be the filtration $(\Gamma_i:=\Gamma\cap G_i)_{i\geq 0}$. Fix any point $f_0\in F$ and let $K:=\mathrm{Stab}_G(f_0)=\{g\in G:g(f_0)=f_0\}$, a closed subgroup of $G$. To complete the proof of our claim, we now show that the groupable nilpair $(K,\Gamma)$ is closed right-discrete. To prove this, we note that the proof of Lemma \ref{lem_aux-for-dou-coset} already gives us that for every $i\in [k]$ the subgroup $KG_{i+1}/G_{i+1}$ of $G/G_{i+1}$ is closed. Thus it only remains to prove that for every $i\in [k]$ the subgroup $K_i\Gamma_i G_{i+1}/(K_i G_{i+1})$ of $G_i/(K_iG_{i+1})$ is discrete. To prove this we shall use again that $\psi$ is equivariant. Hence, by Proposition \ref{prop:embeb-strong-good} there is an injective morphism $\iota:\pi_K(F')\hookrightarrow H/\Gamma$ for some compact nilmanifold $H/\Gamma$. Indeed, by Remark \ref{rem:isometric-embedding}, given any metric $d$ on $H/\Gamma$ we can choose an appropriate metric on $\pi_K(F')$ in such a way that $\iota$ is an isometry. Thus, without loss of generality we apply Theorem \ref{thm:inv-high-ord-latti-intro} with a metrization $D$ such that each $2$-step \textsc{cfr} nilspace is endowed with such an appropriate metric.\footnote{Recall that in Theorem \ref{thm:inv-high-ord-latti-intro} we can choose an arbitrary metrization. The chosen metric for each 2-step \textsc{cfr} nilspace $\pi_K(F')$ is the one that makes $\iota:\pi_K(F')\rightarrow H/\Gamma$ an isometry.} Hence, the Lipschitz map $F:\pi_K(F')\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ can be interpreted as a map $\tilde{F}:\iota(\pi_K(F'))\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$, $\iota(x)\mapsto F(x)$. For any positive integers $j\le \ell$ consider the projection $p_{j,\ell}:\prod_{i=1}^\ell F_i \rightarrow \prod_{i=1}^j F_i$. By the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:LFnstransLie}, the group $C_{j,\ell}:=\{\alpha\in \Theta(\prod_{i=1}^\ell F_i): \forall x,y\in \mathrm{X}, \text{ if } p_{j,\ell}(x)=p_{j,\ell}(y) \text{ then } p_{j,\ell}(\alpha(x))=p_{j,\ell}(\alpha(y))\}$ is a closed subgroup of $\Theta(\prod_{i=1}^\ell F_i)$. Therefore, the group $C_\ell:=\cap_{j=1}^\ell C_{j,\ell}$ is also a closed subgroup of $\Theta(\prod_{i=1}^\ell F_i)$ and hence a Lie group, by Cartan's theorem. Note that $C_\ell = \Theta(\prod_{i=1}^\ell F_i,(F_i)_{i\in [\ell]})$. Let $\widehat{p_{j,\ell}}:\Theta(\prod_{i=1}^\ell F_i,(F_i)_{i\in [\ell]})\rightarrow \Theta(\prod_{i=1}^j F_i)$ be the group homomorphism induced by $p_{j,\ell}$. Then $\widehat{p_{\ell-1,\ell}}:\Theta(\prod_{i=1}^\ell F_i,(F_i)_{i\in [\ell]})\rightarrow \Theta(\prod_{i=1}^{\ell-1} F_i,(F_i)_{i\in [\ell-1]})$ is a well-defined continuous surjective homomorphism.\footnote{The surjectivity follows easily from the fact that given $\alpha\in \Theta(\prod_{i=1}^{\ell-1} F_i,(F_i)_{i\in [\ell-1]})$ the map $(\alpha,\mathrm{id}): (\prod_{i=1}^{\ell-1} F_i)\times F_\ell\rightarrow ( \prod_{i=1}^{\ell-1} F_i)\times F_\ell$ is in $\Theta(\prod_{i=1}^{\ell} F_i,(F_i)_{i\in [\ell]})$.} This defines an inverse system of $k$-step nilpotent Lie groups, whence $\Theta(F,(F_i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}})=\varprojlim \Theta(\prod_{i=1}^\ell F_i,(F_i)_{i\in [\ell]})$ is a pro-Lie group.

Finally, we have to show that the topology on $\Theta(F,(F_i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}})$ as a subset of the set of continuous functions from $F$ to $F$ with the compact-open topology is equal to the topology generated by the limit maps for the inverse system defined by  $\widehat{p_{\ell-1,\ell}}$ for $\ell\in \mathbb{N}$. By \cite[Theorem 46.8]{Mu} the compact-open topology in both $C(F,F)$ and $C(\Theta(\prod_{i=1}^\ell F_i,(F_i)_{i\in [\ell]}),\Theta(\prod_{i=1}^\ell F_i,(F_i)_{i\in [\ell]}))$ for $\ell\in \mathbb{N}$ coincides with the topology of compact convergence. Note that given any metric $d_\ell$ in $\prod_{i=1}^\ell F_i$ for $\ell\in \mathbb{N}$, we can define a bounded equivalent metric just by taking $\max(1,d_\ell(\cdot,\cdot))$. Furthermore, if $d_\ell$ is 1-bounded for all $\ell\in \mathbb{N}$ on $F=\prod_{i<\omega} F_i$ we can define the metric $d_F(x,x'):=\sum_{\ell=1}^\infty \frac{d_\ell(\pi_\ell(x),\pi_\ell(x'))}{2^\ell}$ where $\pi_\ell:F\rightarrow \prod_{i=1}^\ell F_i$ is the projection map. We argue by induction on the step $k$. For $k=1$, it follows from classical results on torsion-free abelian groups that a 1-step sub-nilspace of a free 1-step nilspace is again a free nilspace. Indeed, note that up to the addition of a constant, we can consider $\varphi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_{G'}$ and $\pi_G$ as surjective homomorphisms where we identify $F$ and $F'$ with two abelian groups of the form $\mathbb{Z}^a\times \mathbb{R}^b$ and $\mathbb{Z}^{a'}\times \mathbb{R}^{b'}$ respectively. Thus, the 1-step nilspace $\tilde{F}$ is identified with the following abelian group: $\mathrm{Z}:=\{(f,f')\in (\mathbb{Z}^a\times \mathbb{R}^b)\times (\mathbb{Z}^{a'}\times \mathbb{R}^{b'}):\varphi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_{G'}(f')=\pi_G(f)\}$. But now we have a short exact sequence $0\rightarrow \ker(\pi_G)\rightarrow \mathrm{Z}\rightarrow \mathbb{Z}^{a'}\times \mathbb{R}^{b'}\rightarrow 0$ where $f\in \ker(\pi_G)\mapsto (f,0)\in \mathrm{Z}$ and $(f,f')\in \mathrm{Z}\mapsto f'\in \mathbb{Z}^{a'}\times \mathbb{R}^{b'}$. By \cite[Theorem 3.3]{Mosk} the group $\mathbb{Z}^{a'}\times \mathbb{R}^{b'}$ is projective and thus $\mathrm{Z}$ is isomorphic (as a topological group) to $\mathbb{Z}^{a'}\times \mathbb{R}^{b'}\times \ker(\pi_G)$ by \cite[Theorem 3.5]{Mosk}. The closed subgroup $\ker(\pi_G)\leq \mathbb{Z}^{a}\times \mathbb{R}^b$ is also of the form $\mathbb{Z}^{a''}\times \mathbb{R}^{b''}$. The case $k=1$ follows.

    For $k>1$, we begin by observing that by Lemma \ref{lem:diff-cont} (see also \cite[Proposition A.20]{CGSS-p-hom}) the $(k-1)$-th factor $\tilde{F}_{k-1}$ of $\tilde{F}$ is isomorphic to the fiber-product $F_{k-1}\times_{\mathrm{X}_{k-1}} F'_{k-1}$. Note that we have again a commutative diagram exactly as \eqref{eq:k-stepdiag}, but at step $k-1$ and with $\tilde{F}_{k-1}$. By induction, we can thus assume that $\tilde{F}_{k-1}$ is a free nilspace. Since $\tilde{F}$ is a degree-$k$ extension of this \emph{free} nilspace $\tilde{F}_{k-1}$, by Theorem \ref{thm:splitext} we have $\tilde{F}\cong \tilde{F}_{k-1}\times \mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z})$ where $\mathrm{Z}=\mathrm{Z}_k(\tilde{F})$, the $k$-th structure group of $\tilde{F}$. Moreover $\mathrm{Z}_k(\tilde{F})=\{(z,z')\in \mathrm{Z}_k(F)\times \mathrm{Z}_k(F'): \phi_k(z)=\phi_k'(z')\}$, by Lemma \ref{lem:diff-cont} (where $\mathrm{Z}_k(F)$ and $\mathrm{Z}_k(F')$ are the $k$-th structure groups of $F$ and $F'$ respectively, and $\phi_k:\mathrm{Z}_k(F)\rightarrow \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$, $\phi_k':\mathrm{Z}_k(F')\rightarrow \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$ are the $k$-th structure homomorphisms of $\pi_G$ and $\varphi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_{G'}$ respectively). By the facts for torsion-free abelian groups used in the case $k=1$ above, we have that  $\mathrm{Z}_k(\tilde{F})\cong \mathbb{Z}^a\times \mathbb{R}^b$, for some $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$.

Let $(f,f')\in \tilde{F}$ and $(g,g')\in G\times G'$. Now $(f,f')\in \tilde{F}$ means by definition that $\varphi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\pi_{G'}(f')=\pi_G(f)$, and then clearly $\varphi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\pi_{G'}(g'f')=\pi_G(gf)$, so $G\times G'$ indeed leaves $\tilde{F}$ globally invariant. In particular we have 
$p_2(gf,g'f')=g'f'=g'p_2(f,f')$, and similarly with $p_1$ instead of $p_2$. Hence $G\times G'$ is consistent with both $p_1,p_2$ in the sense of \cite[Definition 1.2]{CGSS}.

We want to prove that $G\times G'$ is a fiber-transitive group on $\tilde{F}$ and that the quotient nilspace $\tilde{F}/(G\times G')$ is a compact nilspace isomorphic (as a compact nilspace) to $\mathrm{X}'$.

Let us check the fiber-transitivity property. We have by assumption that $G$ is fiber-transitive on $F$ and so is $G'$ on $F'$. Suppose that $(f,f'), (h,h')$ in $\tilde{F}$ satisfy $\pi_{i,\tilde{F}} (f,f') = \pi_{i,\tilde{F}}(h,h')$ for some $i\in[k]$ and there is $(g,g')\in G\times G'$ such that $(g,g')(f,f')=(h,h')$. Next, we need to check that if $G,G'$ are fiber-discrete on $F,F'$ respectively then so is $G\times G'$ on $\tilde{F}$. Note that it suffices to check this for the last structure group, as then the result for lower factors follows by induction. Clearly $G_{k}\times G'_k$ is discrete (as a product of two discrete groups). 

To see that $G\times G'$ is fiber-cocompact, recall that by Lemma \ref{lem:diff-cont} we have $\mathrm{Z}_k(\tilde{F})=\{(z,z')\in \mathrm{Z}_k(F)\times \mathrm{Z}_k(F'):\phi_k(z)=\phi'_k(z')\}$ where $\phi_k,\phi_k'$ are the $k$-th structure homomorphisms of $\pi_G$ and $\varphi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_{G'}$ respectively. This is not strictly necessary because if we are in a situation as in Proposition \ref{prop:fiber-prod-of-free}, the fact that $\mathrm{X}'$ is compact forces $\mathrm{X}$ to be compact. Since $\mathrm{X}\cong F/G$, this implies directly that $G$ is fiber-cocompact.}

Moreover, the morphism $p_2:\tilde{F}\rightarrow F'$ is equivariant relative to the actions of $G\times G'$ and $G'$. To see this, note that by induction it suffices to lift g^(j-1) to an element in Theta(F_j,(F_i')_i=1^j) with the desired properties. In fact, since we are considering the graded translations, it is clear that we can find such an element. That is, any element of F_j=(F_i')_i=1^j is of the form (f',f^(j-1))in F_j'times F_j-1 and we know that (g^(j-1))^-1(f_0)=f^(j-1). The translation g^(j)in Theta(F_j,(F_i')_i=1^j) defined as (a,b)in F_j'times F_j-1mapsto(a+f_0-f',g^(j-1)(b)) works. Arguing just as in the proof of Theorem , by the previous paragraph we have that psi'(p_j'^-1(U)) = p_j^-1(psi_j(U)), and the openness follows.

Note that this holds trivially if any of the z_i is 0 (as then the derivative vanishes). Note that it is also clear if tle lfloor k/ellrfloor, since then we have to check that the derivative is Z'-valued, which holds trivially. Thus, the only non-trivial case is when tge lfloor k/ellrfloor+1, in which case we have to check that partial_z_1cdots partial_z_tf is the 0 function. Since fin hom(D_ell(Z),D_k(Z')), viewing the elements z_i as elements of the ell-th term of the filtration defining D_ell(Z) (this term being Z), we see that partial_z_1cdots partial_z_tf takes values in the tell-th term of the filtration D_k(Z'). By assumption tellge ell(lfloor k/ellrfloor+1)ge k+1, so the derivative takes values in the (k+1)-th term of the filtration associated with D_k(Z'), which is \0\ as required. This proves the desired inclusion. \label{rem:Taylor-discrete-app}
Theorem \ref{thm:Taylor-discrete-app} holds even if $F$ has continuous components, provided that $A$ is finitely generated and discrete. In particular, this yields Lemma \ref{lem:Taylor-discrete}.

nodes.statement: First note that the set T:=\min prod_i=1^k Z_ge 0^a_i: |m|le k\ is a finite set. Let us define e_i_0,j_0in prod_i=1^k Z^a_i as the element that equals 1 only at the coordinate indexed by i_0in[k] and j_0in[a_i_0] and 0 otherwise. Note that if mnotin T, by we have partial_e_1,1^m_1,1cdots partial_e_k,a_k^m_k,a_kphi(x)=0. Given two elements m,m'in prod_i=1^k Z_ge 0^a_i, we write mle m' if m_i,jle m'_i,j for all iin[k] and jin[a_i]. We write m<m' if mnot=m' and mle m'. Let Ssubset prod_i=1^k Z_ge 0^a_i be any finite subset. We say that S is simplicial if for every min S and every m'le m we have m'in S. For any function psi:prod_i=1^k Z^a_irightarrow A, let us define the support of psi as follows: \[ supp(psi):=prod_i=1^k Z_ge 0^a_isetminusleft\m in prod_i=1^k Z_ge 0^a_i: partial_e_1,1^m_1,1cdots partial_e_k,a_k^m_k,a_kphi(x)=0 for all xin prod_i=1^k Z^a_iright\. \] Note that if phi:Frightarrow D_k(A) is a morphism then its support is finite, since supp(phi)subset \m in prod_i=1^k Z_ge 0^a_i:|m|le k\. Note also that supp(psi) is always a simplicial set. We shall now prove that if psi:prod_i=1^k Z^a_irightarrow A has finite support then psi(x)=sum_min supp(psi)a_m binomxm for some coefficients a_min A.
